also.hook: Joy Buolamwini is a computer scientist whose research exposed how commercial facial recognition systems perform far worse on darker skinned faces than lighter skinned ones. While a graduate researcher at the MIT Media Lab, she found that some facial analysis software failed to detect her own face until she put on a white mask, an experience that led her to start systematically testing commercial systems for bias. In 2016 she founded the Algorithmic Justice League to combine research, art, and advocacy against harmful bias in AI systems. Her 2018 study Gender Shades, co-authored with Timnit Gebru, tested facial analysis products from IBM, Microsoft, and Face++ using a new benchmark built from images of parliamentarians in African and European countries, and found error rates for darker skinned women far higher than for lighter skinned men. She holds a bachelor's degree in computer science from the Georgia Institute of Technology, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and earned her PhD from the MIT Media Lab. Her work has since informed congressional testimony on facial recognition technology, the 2020 documentary Coded Bias, and her 2023 book Unmasking AI.
also.name: Joy Buolamwini
also.moniker: Computer scientist and founder of the Algorithmic Justice League

also.hook: Timnit Gebru is a computer scientist who has become one of the most prominent voices in AI ethics and accountability. She earned her PhD in computer vision from Stanford University, advised by Fei-Fei Li, after early work in circuit design and audio engineering at Apple. She then completed a postdoctoral fellowship in Microsoft Research's Fairness, Accountability, Transparency and Ethics group before joining Google in 2018, where she co-led the Ethical AI research team with Margaret Mitchell. Gebru left Google in December 2020 after a dispute over a research paper examining the risks of large language models, a departure that drew wide attention to tensions between AI ethics researchers and corporate priorities. In December 2021 she founded the Distributed AI Research Institute, an independent, interdisciplinary institute with researchers based across North America, Europe and Africa that studies the harms of current AI systems and researches alternative approaches. She also co-founded Black in AI, a nonprofit supporting Black researchers and students in artificial intelligence.
also.name: Timnit Gebru

profiles.hook: Whyte became CEO of the American Medical Association in 2025 after nearly seven years as Chief Medical Officer of WebMD, and earlier spent nearly five years at the FDA and over eight years as chief medical expert at Discovery Channel. He holds an MD and an MPH from Harvard.
profiles.name: John Whyte

profiles.hook: Dixon became Chancellor of North Carolina Central University in 2024 after leading Elizabeth City State University for over eight years, including as interim and then permanent Chancellor, and after six years overseeing academic and student affairs system-wide for the 17-campus University of North Carolina system. Her research has focused on college access and summer bridge programs.
profiles.name: Karrie G. Dixon

profiles.hook: Wallace serves as President and CEO of Huston-Tillotson University in Austin, Texas, a historically Black university.

profiles.hook: Arbaugh went from a diving accident that left him paralyzed to becoming, at 29, the first person on Earth to use a brain implant to control a computer in daily life, turning his own recovery into the most closely watched real-world test of whether brain-computer interfaces can restore independence.
profiles.name: Noland Arbaugh
